conventions.convention: Indices start at n=1; vector dimensions are fixed positive integers. Stochastic bounds use Euclidean norms. Probability spaces may vary with n. Little-o means every positive-threshold tail tends to zero; big-O means that for every η>0 some M>0 has limiting upper tail probability at most η.
Vectors combined at index n share a probability space for that n. Independence is unnecessary. A norm-bounded map's actually used composites must be measurable random vectors.
An asymptotic distribution is a weak limit of finite-dimensional laws. Centering and scaling must be specified explicitly; moment convergence is not implied.
Estimator sequences are nonrandomized measurable maps on finite IID product sample spaces into a metric target's Borel sigma-algebra. No parameter-map or estimand measurability is imposed.
Consistency is pointwise: fix θ before taking n→∞, and require the probability of metric error strictly greater than each ε>0 to tend to zero.

The sample-mean theorem assumes a supplied common probability space carrying the infinite IID sequence, a finite first absolute moment at the fixed parameter, and a finite mean estimand throughout the model.
Vector Slutsky requires the second vector's probability limit to be a constant; continuous transformations are defined on the entire finite-dimensional Euclidean product space.

load_bearing.statement: X_n=o_P(1) if every positive Euclidean-norm threshold has tail probability tending to zero. X_n=O_P(1) if for every η>0 there is M>0 such that limsup_n P_n(‖X_n‖₂>M)≤η. Dimensions are fixed and probability spaces may vary with n.

For vectors sharing a probability space at each n, sums preserve o_P(1) and O_P(1). A fixed map satisfying ‖B(u,v)‖₂≤C‖u‖₂‖v‖₂, with its used composites measurable, sends an o_P(1) and an O_P(1) input to o_P(1), and two O_P(1) inputs to O_P(1). Finite-dimensional weak convergence implies O_P(1).

For fixed d,k,m≥1, if X_n⇒X and Y_n−c=o_P(1), where c is constant and X_n,Y_n share a probability space at each n, then (X_n,Y_n)⇒(X,c). Consequently every continuous h:R^(d+k)→R^m satisfies h(X_n,Y_n)⇒h(X,c). No independence is required.
A nonrandomized estimator sequence of ψ is a sequence of measurable maps T_n:(X^n,A^(⊗n))→(T,B(T)), n≥1, with sampling law P_θ^(⊗n) and a metric target.
An estimator sequence is consistent in probability at fixed θ if, for every ε>0, P_θ^(⊗n){d(T_n,ψ(θ))>ε}→0.

For a parametric model, metric-valued estimand and nonrandomized IID estimator sequence, if ψ is not identifiable, there is a pair of observationally equivalent parameters with distinct targets, and no estimator sequence is consistent in probability at both parameters.
For a real Borel observation model with finite mean estimand, a supplied IID sequence at fixed θ with E_θ|X_1|<∞ gives a sample-mean estimator consistent for μ at θ in the finite IID experiments.
A sequence of measurable R^d-valued random elements has asymptotic distribution ν if its laws converge weakly to the Borel probability measure ν.

seams_checked.note: Opened the experiment, model, estimand, observational-equivalence and identifiability definitions. The estimator definition retains the absence of parameter measurability; the impossibility theorem uses equal observation measures and distinct target values, without assuming model injectivity.

The declared page prerequisite is background. Its A-page items contain no direct batch-13 citation. The empirical-process definition supplies its own countability and outer-probability conventions and does not extend finite-dimensional stochastic notation to nonmeasurable suprema.

The functional CLT cites def-asymptotic-distribution in F1 and step 9.1 only for finite-dimensional projections. Process-level convergence is separately defined and proved with outer expectations; the finite-dimensional definition is not used as a process-convergence theorem.

M/Z definitions retain data-measurable estimators and measurable residuals. Consistency proofs use fixed positive metric-error thresholds. The Z definition explicitly reconciles its chosen finite-dimensional norm with the Euclidean little-o convention through norm equivalence.

Delta-method and Z-asymptotic-linearity uses retain fixed finite dimensions, measurable composites, weak-convergence boundedness, and constant-limit Slutsky. Their product uses are measurable scalar multiplication, and remainder convergence is established before applying Slutsky.

MLE and chi-square-calibration citations preserve Euclidean stochastic bounds, finite-dimensional weak-convergence boundedness and constant-limit Slutsky. Product uses concern measurable finite-dimensional scores, coefficients and quadratic forms; no independence between estimators and scores is inferred.
